records.quote:
forgetting every injunction to silence
I screamed and screamed and screamed as my nerves gave way and the
walls quivered about me
records.paraphrase: The narrator screams uncontrollably at the horrifying future vision.

records.quote:
Garish daylight showed
only squalor and alienage and the noxious elephantiasis of climbing,
spreading stone where the moon had hinted of loveliness and elder
magic
records.paraphrase: The narrator contrasts the beautiful nighttime appearance of the city with its squalid daytime reality.

records.quote:
It spread over the old man, too, whether from
the same source or because of his fear and vehemence, and I saw him
shrivel and blacken as he lurched near and strove to rend me with
vulturine talons.
records.paraphrase: The old man shrivels and blackens under the moonlight, transforming physically.

records.quote:
Then the floor gave way at last, and I slid gaspingly down into the
nighted chamber below, choking with cobwebs and half-swooning with
terror.
records.paraphrase: The house collapses as the narrator falls through the floor.

records.quote:
I saw the heavens verminous with strange
flying things, and beneath them a hellish black city of giant stone
terraces with impious pyramids flung savagely to the moon
records.paraphrase: A vision of the future shows a monstrous city with strange flying things and alien people.

records.quote:
I had found instead only a sense of horror and
oppression which threatened to master, paralyze, and annihilate me.
records.paraphrase: The narrator describes his emotional horror and oppression upon arriving in New York.

records.quote:
he flouted the sanctity of
things as great as space and time and that he put to strange uses
the rites of sartain half-breed red Indians once encamped upon this
hill
records.paraphrase: The host describes the ancestor manipulating space and time using rites learned from local Indians.

records.quote:
this city of stone and
stridor is not a sentient perpetuation of Old New York as London is
of Old London and Paris of Old Paris, but that it is in fact quite
dead, its sprawling body imperfectly embalmed and infested with
queer animate things
records.paraphrase: The narrator concludes that the city is dead and infested with alien animate things.

records.quote:
I saw the gleam of a tomahawk as it cleft the
rending wood. I did not move, for I could not; but watched dazedly
as the door fell in pieces to admit a colossal, shapeless influx of
inky substance starred with shining, malevolent eyes.
records.paraphrase: The door is broken open and a shapeless mass with glowing eyes floods in to seize the old man.

records.quote:
he bargained with them and exchanged the free access of
his grounds for the exact inwardness of what they did; larning that
their grandfathers got part of their custom from red ancestors and
part from an old Dutchman in the time of the States-General
records.paraphrase: The squire investigates and negotiates to learn the origins and workings of the secret rites.

criteria.rationale: The story is supernatural/occult fantasy. The ancestor's manipulation of space and time is framed as arcane rites and 'magic' learned from Indians and a Dutchman, not as scientific fact, theory, or speculative science. No natural process or discipline is materially represented.
The temporal visions are produced by occult rites and the necromancer's gestures, not by any device, engineered system, or invention. No technology materially affects the setting or outcome.

The core spectacle is temporal displacement: the host reveals visions of the remote past and a horrifying speculative future city with strange flying things, driving the story's central experience even if achieved by magical means.

One could read the future vision of a swarming alien-populated New York as extrapolation of the narrator's xenophobic disgust at the city's present demographics, but this is a mystical projection rather than reasoned development from an identifiable premise, so materiality and interpretation are uncertain.

The squire's bargaining and learning of the rites is occult inquiry and negotiation, not observation, hypothesis testing, measurement, or evidential revision. No systematic scientific reasoning materially drives understanding or action.

The future vision presents a substantially nonordinary environment with strange flying things and alien inhabitants, and a shapeless inky entity with malevolent eyes intrudes, but these are supernatural rather than clearly extraterrestrial or interdimensional, leaving the cosmic-environment reading uncertain.

The house collapses and a supernatural horde destroys the necromancer, but this is a localized, personal-scale catastrophe rather than a large-scale disaster; the apocalyptic future vision hints at wider ruin but is not established as an actual or impending large-scale event.

candidates.description: The ancestor/necromancer's discovery that the human will, augmented by rites acquired from local Indians and European occultists, exercises dominance over space and time, allowing manipulation of temporal windows and the summoning of past and future scenes. This governs the entire encounter, the visions shown to the narrator, and the story's climactic catastrophe.

novelty.rationale: The premise posits a totalizing difference from the empirical norm: a plot of ground where the will can flout the sanctity of space and time, opening windows onto past and future epochs and physically altering bodies. This world-altering capacity restructures the story's reality.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The story gestures at a quasi-systematic account (arts, discoveries, bargained knowledge, an Oxford-educated squire and a Parisian chymist-astrologer, a philosophy that the world is 'the smoke of our intellects'). But the mechanism is framed as necromancy, 'magic,' and the powers manifest as vengeful spirits and supernatural transformation rather than an immanent, nonsupernatural logic. The account is closer to supernatural horror than an imaginary science, so cognitive validation is genuinely mixed.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The manipulation of time and its consequences drive the whole second half of the narrative: the demonstration of past and future visions, the narrator's scream breaking the injunction, the summoning of the vengeful horde, and the destruction of the old man and the house.

estrangement.rationale: The reader-facing contrast between the moonlit-beautiful and daylight-squalid city, and the framing of New York as a dead, embalmed corpse infested with animate things, estranges the familiar metropolis. The visions of past foliage and a monstrous future city extend this estrangement across time.

candidates.description: The narrator's conceit that New York is not a living continuation of Old New York but is 'quite dead,' an imperfectly embalmed corpse infested with alien animate things.

novelty.rationale: The 'dead city' is presented as a subjective, poetic-mystical perception rather than an established world-altering fact; it reads as metaphor and mood more than a totalizing objective difference from the empirical norm.

cognitive_validation.rationale: No systematic, immanent account is offered for how a city is literally dead and embalmed; it is delivered as a felt 'unwhisperable secret' with no explanatory mechanism.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The dead-city motif frames the narrator's alienation and motivates his nocturnal wanderings, but the driving plot mechanism is the necromancer's temporal power, not the dead-city conceit itself.

estrangement.rationale: The recasting of a real modern city as a dead, embalmed corpse infested with 'queer animate things' defamiliarizes the empirical New York, an estranging poetic reframing.
